analysis.one_liner: Reinstates Superfund taxes on oil, chemicals, and large corporate profits to pay for toxic-waste cleanups.
analysis.headline: The Superfund Polluter Pays Act, introduced with 5 House cosponsors, was never taken up by the Ways and Means Committee and received no vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have revived two expired taxes to refill the Superfund, the federal fund that pays to clean up abandoned toxic-waste sites: a per-barrel tax on crude oil and imported petroleum products raised to 16.3 cents, and a per-ton tax on roughly 40 industrial chemicals, both rising with inflation through 2025. It would also add a new 0.12% surtax on corporate profits above $3.13 million, also inflation-adjusted, through 2026. The money would go to the Superfund trust fund rather than to general taxpayer funds.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people living near contaminated sites benefit from faster, better-funded cleanups, and taxpayers generally benefit because cleanup costs would be covered by oil, chemical, and large profitable corporations rather than general revenue.

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates and raises the per-barrel petroleum tax to 16.3 cents and extends it through 2025, restoring a dedicated revenue stream to the Superfund trust fund.
Imposes a 0.12% tax on corporate taxable income above $3.13 million, which falls only on larger profitable corporations and funnels the revenue into Superfund financing.
Inflation-adjusts the petroleum rate, chemical fees, and the corporate surtax threshold, so the fund would not quietly lose purchasing power over time.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and petroleum refiners/importers pay the per-barrel tax; chemical manufacturers and importers pay the per-ton chemical fees; and profitable corporations above the income threshold pay the new surtax. Some of these costs may be passed to consumers in fuel and chemical-product prices.

drawbacks.text: Excise taxes on oil and chemicals are partly passed through to consumers in the form of higher fuel and product prices, hitting households and energy-intensive manufacturers.

The corporate surtax excludes regulated investment companies and real estate investment trusts and allows no net-operating-loss offset, which critics could argue is arbitrary in its carve-outs and design.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a dedicated funding stream for toxic-site cleanups paid largely by the industries most tied to hazardous waste, reducing the burden on general taxpayers. The main cost is modest price pass-through on fuels and chemical products and a small but broad new tax on larger corporations; the policy tradeoff appears heavily favorable to the public, though the bill was never debated or refined in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on introduction day and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote; it died there when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The Superfund Polluter Pays Act was introduced on April 20, 2021, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
No further action was recorded on the bill after the initial referral — no markup, no hearing, no committee vote, no floor consideration.
The bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without ever receiving a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and petroleum companies, chemical manufacturers, and large profitable corporations were better off because the bill never became law, avoiding the reinstated per-barrel and per-chemical excise taxes and the new 0.12% corporate surtax. Taxpayers and communities near toxic sites lost the chance at a dedicated cleanup funding source, keeping cleanup costs on general revenue instead of polluting industries.

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Superfund Polluter Pays Act on April 20, 2021.

for.name: Reps. Earl Blumenauer, Bill Pascrell, and Donald McEachin
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

for.name: Two additional House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as additional cosponsors after introduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral but took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote was held on the bill.

against.name: Oil and petroleum industry
against.role: Would-be payers of the reinstated per-barrel Superfund tax
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against reinstating lapsed Superfund excise taxes, which Congress had allowed to expire in 1995.

sides.party_line_note: All five cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill sat with no recorded action after referral in a committee dominated by members of both parties who took no step to advance it.

industries.note: Would have paid a reinstated and raised 16.3-cent-per-barrel tax on crude and petroleum products through 2025, restoring a levy that expired in 1995. The industry's interest in blocking it ran against the public's interest in a funded Superfund.

Would have resumed per-ton excise fees on roughly 40 listed chemicals (e.g., benzene, mercury, sulfuric acid), also inflation-adjusted. These fees fund cleanups of the hazardous sites such chemicals helped create.
A new 0.12% surtax on income above $3.13 million would have applied broadly to large corporations (excluding RICs and REITs), adding a modest cost on top of regular corporate tax.
A replenished Superfund trust fund would increase federal demand for hazardous-site assessment and cleanup contractors, while accelerating cleanups for affected communities.
